newsitem.title: UK: FUTURES EXPAND ROLE IN UK GAS TRADE AS VOLUMES RISE.
newsitem.headline: FUTURES EXPAND ROLE IN UK GAS TRADE AS VOLUMES RISE.

text.p: The futures market will become a key part of natural gas trading in Britain if a recent pick up in volumes on the International Petroleum Exchange's (IPE) gas contract is sustained, industry sources said on Monday.
The futures contract got off to a stuttering start after its launch six months ago, and went completely untraded on several days.
But liquidity on the contract has increased in recent weeks, with trading volumes hitting a record 960 lots, or nearly a million therms a day in late July.

"It's already an essential part of the market for a lot of people as it offers certain things like anonymity that the OTC (over-the-counter) market doesn't offer," said one trader active in the U.K. market.
Last Friday, trading was extended by three hours, cutting out a midday closure, and a new current month contract started trading.

Traders said that the introduction of "day ahead" trading and continued high volumes could allow the IPE to be used as an index for pricing physical deals, a role currently filled by industry publications.
"If it continues with high levels of activity then it will let us use the IPE as an index to price deal against instead of using publications," said one trader for a major U.K. shipper.
"While it was thin people were reluctant to use it because it could be easily manipulated," he added.

The IPE said it may make more changes to the contract, and is looking ahead to launching a European contract when the Interconnector pipeline -- linking the British gas grid with European networks -- comes onstream next year.
"We are anticipating more changes such as quarterly and daily contracts...but everything is being done in close consultation with industry," said a spokeswoman for the IPE.

Richard Ward, head of business development at the IPE, said at the launch of the contract said that he hoped to see daily trade expanding to around 2000 lots or two million therms a day by the end of the first quarter 1998.
Some 10 to 15 gas companies trade gas regularly on the IPE. The majority are shippers, who transport gas from North Sea beach terminals to end-users.

Brokers working on the IPE contract are hoping to attract new players into the market, including North Sea producers, power generators, and regional electricity companies which are active in the spot market.
"We could do with another 10 or 20 players especially producers and generators," said one IPE floor broker.

"There are still a lot of companies whose management has not agreed to use it. They are unsure about the liabilities, and unwilling to pay the margins...but I think soon people will look at it as something not just supply/demand led and will use it to hedge risk," he added.
The London Clearing House (LCH), which is counterparty to every trade struck on the IPE, has already cut margins twice on the natural gas contract since its launch as liquidity increased.
"We're extremely pleased to see the volumes going through in recent weeks. Open interest has been building up and that is good for liquidity," said an LCH spokesman.
Open interest on the contract was 5575 lots or 5.5 million therms on Monday.
The LCH spokesman said margins would be reviewed again "fairly soon".
"Things are moving in the right direction to encourage more people in...soon it will be accepted as part and parcel of the business," said one gas trader.
